title: Persuasion or Manipulation?
objective: After this level you can tell persuasion that gives you good reasons from manipulation that works around them.
summary: Rational persuasion gives you reasons; coercion forces you; manipulation works around your judgment through trickery or pressure. Feelings alone don't make it manipulation.

cards.headline: Irving wants Tonya to choose X. His reasons didn't work. Now what?
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy opens its entry on manipulation with this pair. Irving could charm Tonya, make her feel guilty, nag her, or stoke a fear until X looks better. Each tactic, the entry says, could reasonably be called manipulation.

cards.headline: Three ways to change a mind
cards.body: Philosophers usually set manipulation apart from two other kinds of influence. Rational persuasion gives you reasons. Coercion forces you. Manipulation is neither. One view pictures a scale of pressure: persuasion exerts none, coercion the most, and manipulation sits somewhere in between.

cards.headline: Around your judgment, not through it
cards.body: Accounts of manipulation fall into rough families. One says it bypasses your reasoning. Another treats it as trickery, planting misleading beliefs or associations. A third sees pressure: guilt trips and nagging make saying no costly. What they share is the route. Persuasion goes through your judgment; manipulation goes around it.

cards.headline: Feelings aren't the dividing line
cards.body: Philosophers find it implausible that every appeal to emotion is manipulative. So the test isn't whether you felt something. Ask instead: is this giving me a reason I could check, or pushing me to decide before I can? Taking time to weigh the grounds is Level 1's suspended judgment, put to work.

mascot.line: People mix up Level 72 and this one. That was about arguments. This is about the route: through your judgment, or around it.

cards.headline: Manipulation: named
learned: Trickery and pressure are its common routes
Emotion alone doesn't make it manipulation

questions.prompt: Match each kind of influence with what it does.
questions.explanation: Rational persuasion gives you reasons, and coercion forces you. Manipulation goes around your judgment instead of through it.

questions.prompt: On the pressure view, how do guilt trips and nagging manipulate?

options.label: They make saying no costly until you give in
They give you better reasons to agree
options.rationale: Reasons would be persuasion, not pressure.

options.label: They plant a false belief in you
They force you to agree with an outright threat

questions.explanation: Pressure works by making refusal costly, not by giving reasons.

questions.prompt: The habit from John Dewey that best protects you against "decide right now" pressure is _____.

options.label: counting how many people agree
options.rationale: Popularity isn't a ground for a belief.

options.label: trusting your first feeling
options.rationale: Pressure works best on first feelings.

questions.explanation: Dewey's suspended judgment means holding off until you've weighed the grounds, which is exactly what pressure tries to prevent.
